output: Generating candidate transition-state structures from molecular connectivity offers a route to computational reaction characterization. We present a method that generates 50 candidate structures per reaction from atom-mapped reactant and product SMILES. Among 40 test reactions, 36 yielded at least one optimized candidate with a single imaginary frequency. For 28 reactions, bidirectional intrinsic reaction coordinate calculations were completed and the resulting endpoints matched the expected identities. On this endpoint-validated subset, the mean absolute error in electronic activation energies, ΔE‡, was 1.8 kcal mol−1. These results establish candidate-generation and pathway-validation performance within the tested set; free-energy barriers, experimental rates, and applicability to other reaction classes remain unassessed.
Each optimized structure has one imaginary frequency; the IRC calculations have not yet been performed.

Retrospectively selecting, for each reaction, the candidate with the lowest RMSD to the known reference transition state yielded a median RMSD of 0.14 Å, quantifying the best available generated candidates under reference-informed selection without evaluating reference-free deployment ranking performance.
The computed electronic activation energy, ΔE‡, was 50.2 kJ mol−1 relative to the separated reactants.

Of the 50 submitted reactions, 35 produced at least one optimized candidate, and 25 of these 35 passed endpoint validation. The conditional endpoint-validation fraction was therefore 71.4% (25/35), corresponding to an overall fraction of 50.0% (25/50).
For 16 of 20 evaluated Diels–Alder reactions, the model yielded candidates meeting the specified structural criterion, with other reaction families and IRC connectivity remaining unassessed.

Rapid candidate generation can facilitate reaction screening. The workflow generated candidates for 12 cycloaddition reactions, with eight reactions passing the stated optimization and endpoint checks. These results support its promise within the tested set.

Developing ligands for Ni-catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura coupling motivates testing whether knowledge from Pd catalysis can guide a system represented by a smaller data set. The study used transfer learning to combine extensive Pd catalysis data with a smaller Ni/Sadphos data set and propose Sadphos ligands for the Ni-catalyzed reaction. Predicted ligand utility was examined through synthesis applications, including a gram-scale demonstration. Density functional theory calculations assessed a mechanistic relationship between the catalytic systems, providing a chemical perspective on the transfer-learning approach.
